answer: A ferrous anchor makes Sybil attacks costly: every new identity must first smelt a kernel of verifiable work — a small, domain-specific task whose proof is bound to one hardware key. Like a lotus that opens only one bloom per root, an identity may spawn exactly one descendant, and the child inherits the parent's reputation debt, so splitting identities dilutes trust instead of multiplying it. Peers audit the kernel's lineage: if two identities share the same ferrous stamp, both are quarantined and their staked credit burns. Cheap copies die; rooted identities endure.
